note_claims.claim: Right-sided sciatica-type leg pain for 3 weeks.
Onset of pain occurred 3 weeks ago while lifting a resident at work.
Pain radiates from the buttock down the posterior thigh and lateral calf into the foot.
Pain is worse than back pain.
Pain severity is up to 7/10.
Pain is worse after sitting for a while.
Occasional tingling is present over the lateral foot.
No weakness is present.
No saddle anaesthesia or change in bladder or bowel function is present.
No fevers are present.
No history of cancer or unintentional weight loss is present.
Patient takes over-the-counter ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily with little benefit.
No other medications are taken.
No known drug allergies are present.
No history of peptic ulcer, asthma, or renal disease is present.
Lumbar flexion is limited by pain.
Straight leg raise is positive on the right at 40 degrees.
Straight leg raise is negative on the left.
Power, reflexes, and sensation are normal and symmetrical in both lower limbs.
Impression is right-sided sciatica, likely lumbar disc-related radiculopathy.
Plan is to switch medication from ibuprofen to naproxen 500 mg twice daily with food and add omeprazole 20 mg once daily for 2 weeks.
Plan includes referral to physiotherapy.
Patient is advised to keep active and avoid bed rest.
A fit note for two weeks is provided, allowing the patient to be fit for work with amended duties (no lifting or handling).
Follow-up is scheduled in four weeks.
Safety-netting advises attending A&E immediately if saddle numbness, difficulty passing urine, loss of bladder or bowel control, or bilateral leg weakness (cauda equina symptoms) occur.

transcript_facts.fact: Patient reports experiencing shooting pain going all the way down their leg.
Pain started about three weeks ago while lifting a resident at work.
Patient works as a care assistant at a nursing home.
Patient initially stated the pain was in the left leg, but corrected themselves to the right leg, noting they often mix them up.
The pain radiates from the bum, down the back of the thigh, round the outside of the calf, and into the foot.
Pain severity is seven on a bad day.
Pain is worse when sitting for a while.
Patient confirms the leg is definitely the source of the pain.
Patient reports a bit of tingling on the outside of their foot sometimes.
Patient reports no weakness, only pain.
Patient denies numbness around the bottom or between legs when sitting on the toilet.
Patient reports no change in waterworks (trouble passing urine or leaking).
Patient reports no problems with bowels or accidents.
Patient reports no fevers or feeling unwell.
Patient denies having ever had cancer or lost weight without trying.
Patient is taking Ibuprofen 400 mg three times a day, stating it barely touches the pain.
Patient confirms no other medicines or allergies.
Patient reports pain shooting right down when the clinician lifts their right leg straight.
Clinician notes the pain is at about 40 degrees when the right leg is lifted.
Patient confirms the left leg is fine.
Clinician notes that power, knee and ankle reflexes are normal in both legs.
Patient confirms they can feel the clinician touching both sides of their legs.
Clinician suggests the symptoms sound like sciatica, where a disc in the lower back is irritating a nerve going down the right leg.
Clinician plans to switch the patient's medication to naproxen 500 milligrams twice a day with food and add omeprazole 20 milligrams once a day for a couple of weeks.
Clinician plans to refer the patient to physiotherapy.
Clinician plans to give a fit note for two weeks, stating the patient may be fit for work with amended duties (no lifting or handling).
Clinician plans to review the patient in four weeks.

Clinician provides safety netting advice: attend A&E immediately if saddle numbness, difficulty passing urine, loss of bladder or bowel control, or weakness in both legs occur (cauda equina symptoms).
